analysis.one_liner: Caps fossil fuel emissions through annual permit auctions and returns all auction proceeds as equal quarterly dividend checks to lawful residents.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action in the 115th Congress, dying in committee with 36 Democratic cosponsors and none from the Republican majority.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require oil refineries, coal mines, and natural gas suppliers to buy federal carbon permits at auction, with the number of permits shrinking each year until emissions are 80% below 2005 levels by 2050. Every dollar raised at auction, minus administration costs, would be split evenly and sent as a tax-free quarterly check to every lawful U.S. resident with a Social Security number. Because permits are auctioned rather than given away, the money from fossil fuel sales flows to households instead of to the companies emitting the carbon.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households. The dividend is the same for every eligible person, so a household's energy costs (which rise with a carbon cap) are offset more than fully for anyone who burns less than an average share of fossil fuel — which describes most low- and middle-income households. Public health also benefits as emissions fall, and border fees would shield domestic manufacturers from undercutting by countries without carbon rules.

how_it_helps.text: Auctions all carbon permits to fossil fuel suppliers and appropriates the full proceeds, minus administrative costs, to a Healthy Climate Trust Fund that pays an equal quarterly dividend to each eligible individual; the dividend is excluded from gross income so it is not taxed.

Sets a declining cap — permits fall each year from 12.5% below 2005 emissions in 2019 to 80% below by 2050 — so the total amount of CO2 from oil, coal, and natural gas sold in U.S. markets shrinks on a fixed schedule.

Limits auction participation to covered entities, caps how many permits a single company can hold to prevent hoarding and speculation, and charges violators a penalty of three times the market value of missing permits.

Imposes fees on imports of carbon-intensive goods (steel, aluminum, cement, glass, paper, chemicals) from countries without equivalent carbon rules, and pays matching rebates to U.S. exporters, protecting domestic manufacturers.

Requires the EPA to regulate all other greenhouse gases — excluding gases from livestock production — in stages reaching 100% of those emissions within 10 years, with Clean Air Act citizen-suit enforcement available.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers — refineries, petroleum importers, coal mines, coal importers, and natural gas suppliers and processors — who must buy permits for every ton of carbon in the fuels they sell, with a shrinking supply of permits pushing the price up over time. They can be expected to pass much of that cost to consumers through higher gasoline, heating, and electricity prices, which is why the dividend is designed to exceed those costs for most households. Energy-intensive manufacturers face higher input costs, softened by import fees and export rebates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, coal, and natural gas producers

drawbacks.text: Higher fossil fuel prices are the point of the cap, and companies can pass them to consumers immediately while dividends arrive quarterly — a squeeze for households living paycheck to paycheck, and for the highest-energy-using households the dividend may not cover the increase.
The bill contains no dedicated transition assistance for coal miners, oil and gas workers, or fossil-fuel-dependent communities, whose industries would shrink under the declining cap.
Dividends go only to lawful residents with valid Social Security numbers, excluding undocumented immigrants who also face higher energy prices.

The EPA's regulation of non-auction greenhouse gases explicitly excludes gases attributable to livestock production, a major emissions source, and requires the agency to weigh international competitiveness when setting those rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is strongly progressive: an equal per-person dividend funded entirely by fossil fuel sellers leaves most low- and middle-income households financially ahead, while heavy energy users and the companies causing the emissions bear the net cost. The genuine costs are near-term price increases on gasoline and heating before dividends arrive, real losses concentrated in fossil fuel regions with no dedicated worker relief in the bill, and the omission of agricultural emissions from the EPA mandate. On the whole it is one of the more direct ways to cut emissions while paying households rather than giving permits away for free.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees in January 2018, sent to an Energy and Commerce subcommittee days later, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Beyer introduced the bill on January 29, 2018, with 25 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, for provisions in its jurisdiction, to the Committee on Ways and Means.
On February 2, 2018, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Environment.
All 36 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on.
No further action of any kind was recorded for the remainder of the 115th Congress, which ended January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and major industrial fossil fuel users are better off: no cap, no permit auctions, and no compliance costs were ever imposed, while households received no dividends and emissions followed no mandated decline.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 25 original cosponsors from among House Democrats.

for.name: 36 of 193 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all cosponsors were Democrats.

sides.party_line_note: All 36 cosponsors were House Democrats and the bill drew no Republican support; the Republican-controlled Energy and Commerce Committee never moved it past subcommittee referral.

industries.industry: Oil, coal, and natural gas producers and suppliers
industries.note: The bill makes refineries, coal mines, and gas suppliers buy auctioned permits for every ton of carbon in the fuels they sell, with a supply shrinking to 80% below 2005 levels by 2050 and a penalty of three times market value for noncompliance. The industry's cost is precisely the public's dividend, so the bill's interests run directly against the industry's.

industries.industry: Energy-intensive manufacturers (steel, aluminum, cement, glass, paper, chemicals)
industries.note: Higher fuel and input costs under the cap are offset by carbon equivalency fees on competing imports and rebates paid to exporters of carbon-intensive goods, cushioning the sector against foreign competition. Consumers could still see higher prices on some manufactured goods.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and carbon capture developers
industries.note: A rising permit price makes wind, solar, and efficiency cheaper relative to fossil fuels, and the bill issues extra permits to anyone who verifiably captures and sequesters CO2, directly paying for carbon removal.
